title: Origen Therapeutics weekly results sync - latency & throughput vs baseline
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review lab benchmark results comparing Redwood inference stack to the baseline provider. Discussion covered p50/p95 latencies, tokens/sec throughput at different batch sizes, quantization impacts, KV/prefix cache behavior, and cost-per-token. Agreed on next steps: share annotated spreadsheet, run 24-hour soak at concurrency 32, deliver tuned config and error logs, and schedule a technical deep dive next week.
next_steps: Redwood (Maya): share tuned inference config + runbook and backend logs by 2025-09-08
Redwood (Jordan): send updated pricing spreadsheet and pilot contract template by 2025-09-06
Origen (Rajiv): provide full request distribution and workload samples for 24-hour soak by 2025-09-07
Schedule SE deep-dive demo (60m) week of 2025-09-08 — tentative 2025-09-10 14:00 UTC
action_items: Maya Chen: upload tuned config, kernel selection notes, and perf logs to shared drive by 2025-09-08
Jordan Patel: send cost comparison spreadsheet (redwood vs baseline) and short one-pager on fallbacks by 2025-09-06

transcript:
HEADER: 2025-09-04 15:00 UTC - Duration 42m - Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Owen (Redwood), Dr. Elena Santos (CTO, Origen), Rajiv (ML Eng), Lisa (PM)

AUTO-SUMMARY: quick review of week-6 lab benchmarks, redwood outperforms baseline on p50/p95 and throughput when using tuned batching + prefix cache. Action: share config, run soak, schedule deep technical dive.

00:00 Jordan: okay hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Thursday afternoon, should be about 40 minutes, quick agenda — results, tuning notes, next steps.
00:14 Dr. Elena: thanks Jordan, busy week so appreciate it. we mostly want to confirm the numbers you sent this morning and understand risk at scale.
00:27 Rajiv: yes and specifically tail latency under burst load, we've seen some spikes with the baseline provider that break our SLA.
00:35 Maya: great - we ran a few targeted scenarios this week. i'll take you through the spreadsheet, highlight p50/p95 across the three workloads you gave (convo-short, convo-long, batch-embed). please forgive any typos in the doc, i exported raw.
00:55 Jordan: quick housekeeping: baseline in our tests = "MegaCloud" managed endpoint with default batching. our Redwood config used int8 quantization on the Llama-family variant, continuous batching with 150ms max window, and prefix cache enabled for recent prompts.
01:12 Lisa: can you repeat the numbers for p95 on convo-long? the sheet had a few columns.
01:20 Maya: sure — convo-long p50: 38 ms on redwood, p95: 210 ms. baseline p50: 120 ms, p95: 540 ms. those are median values over 10-minute runs at concurrency 16, batch size distribution approx 1-8.
01:44 Rajiv: wow p95 down to 210 — that's a big delta. what's the error rate at that config? we care about the 99+ errors.
01:53 Maya: error rate on redwood tests was 0.08% timeouts/retries, baseline had 0.6% at the same concurrency. note baseline showed increased 5xxs once we pushed concurrency >24.
02:10 Dr. Elena: and throughput? tokens per second?
02:14 Maya: tokens/sec (convo-long): redwood ~1,120 tokens/sec at sustained runs, baseline ~420 tokens/sec with the managed endpoint and default batching. that was with batch window 150ms; when we increased the batch window to 300ms baseline throughput improved to ~680 but p95 also increased.
02:33 Jordan: important: our measurements include prefix caching — for templates that repeat the same leading few hundred tokens, p95 dropped another ~35% and tokens/sec increased because cache hits avoid re-computation of earlier layers.
02:48 Rajiv: is the prefix cache transparent to your API or does it require application changes?
02:52 Maya: it's server-side, transparent but we recommend idempotent prompt shapes; also we expose a cache-control header if you want to opt-out.
03:05 Lisa: what about cost per million tokens — you sent a cost table but just to align numbers for procurement.
03:11 Jordan: right, quick high-level: during pilot config (int8 + caching + batching) effective cost was about $3.20 per million tokens on Redwood; baseline effective cost in our test was $5.60 per million when accounting for retries and higher latency-induced lower throughput. these are approximate pilot numbers, will send a detailed sheet.
03:31 Rajiv: curious about model variants — were you using same model weights across both? are we apples-to-apples?
03:36 Maya: we tried to keep parity — same open-architecture weights, minor differences in compiler kernels. baseline used default vendor kernel set, we used optimized kernels and a custom fused attention path that reduces per-token compute for shorter sequences. i'll add kernel notes to the config bundle.
03:56 Dr. Elena: okay, what are the failure modes you saw? any correctness or decoding differences?
04:03 Maya: decoding/numeric outputs were within expected variance; no systemic drift. one quirk: baseline had increased decoding latency variability under bursty traffic which led to timeouts at client-side. Redwood's graceful backpressure and fallback to lower precision variants reduced visible timeouts.
04:24 Rajiv: you mentioned lower precision — did you test fp16 vs int8? how big is the perf delta?
04:29 Maya: yes — fp16 baseline for redwood was p95 ~290 ms, int8 tuned was p95 ~210 ms. throughput improved ~18% moving to int8 for this model family. quality tests (bleu/qa checks) showed negligible regression for our eval prompts.
04:46 Jordan: also note the quantized variant used a different kernel selection which is why kernel notes matter — some HW combos see larger win.
04:55 Lisa: any caveats for private deployment or VPC? we may need to run this inside our VPC later.
05:01 Maya: we validated similar performance on our private node image in the lab — the main differences are network egress and KMS latencies for key management. those added ~10-30 ms in some encrypted path tests; we included that in a separate column in the sheet.
05:18 Rajiv: super — can you run a 24-hour soak at concurrency 32 with our traffic shape? that's our next gating item.
05:23 Jordan: yes we can, but we wanted to talk about cost and potential burst capacity if we need headroom. running long soak with larger concurrency will consume commit faster.
05:33 Dr. Elena: second, what about rolling degradation? will the system fall back to a cheaper variant automatically? we need predictable SLAs.
05:41 Maya: we demonstrated automatic fallback: when load breaches our configured SLO, Redwood can route to a compatible lower-cost model variant or a cached-response tier; fallback is configurable per-route. it preserves a 99% availability window while degrading some latency or token quality depending on the policy you pick.
05:59 Rajiv: during the tests did you observe any KV cache thrashing? our prompts sometimes change user names in the prefix which could reduce cache hit rates.
06:07 Maya: yes, in samples with highly dynamic prefixes cache hit rate fell to 12% which reduced the perf gap vs baseline. for your templates where we saw stable prefixes hit rate was ~72%. if your traffic is dynamic we can discuss prefix normalization strategies.
06:25 Lisa: normalization would be a product change on our side but doable.
06:30 Jordan: back to numbers — one more scenario: batch-embed workload (large parallel requests). redwood achieved 2,800 embeddings/sec at batch size 64 (quantized float path) vs baseline ~900/sec. baseline vendor throttled at higher concurrency which caused retries.
06:50 Rajiv: what's the memory footprint on the GPU for int8 + cache? do you need extra GPUs for headroom?
06:56 Maya: memory footprint dropped ~22% with int8. KV cache uses separate host memory with GPU pinned buffers; for your dataset the test ran comfortably on a single A100-80GB equivalent per shard. we'll provide exact sizing estimates.
07:15 Dr. Elena: any security concerns captured during these runs? audit logs, KMS latency already mentioned.
07:22 Jordan: we also captured audit log throughput and didn't see exceedance. KMS round-trip adds a small hiccup for cold starts; we recommend HSM-backed rolling keys — we can detail SAML and SOC2 posture in the security docs.
07:36 Rajiv: error patterns — are 5xxs correlated with GC/IO or pure compute saturation?
07:41 Maya: mostly compute queuing on the baseline. on Redwood we saw more predictable queuing; the small percentage of errors aligned with network hiccups during multi-region tests. we'll include the logs.
07:58 Lisa: great, procurement will want a clear cost delta and a pilot success criteria doc.
08:04 Jordan: we'll send a one-pager: success = sustained p95 < 300ms for convo-long, throughput >= 1000 tps, error rate < 0.2% over 24h soak, cost delta within target.
08:17 Rajiv: that sounds reasonable. what about Canary rollouts if we choose to go live?
08:22 Maya: we support canary routing per user-segment, A/B splitting, and automatic rollback on eval regressions. we can demo the rollout console in the deep dive.
08:33 Dr. Elena: okay let's call out any blockers.
08:36 Rajiv: the only blocker is we need the 24-hour soak results with our exact traffic shape and the associated logs for debugging spikes.
08:43 Jordan: action items noted. we'll aim to start the soak tomorrow morning.
08:48 Lisa: timeline for results?
08:50 Jordan: 24 hours + 8 hours to collate logs and produce a short report -> target 2025-09-06 evening.
09:01 Maya: quick note — we plan to test two tuning knobs during the soak: 1) reduce batching window to 100ms to see tail latency effects, 2) enable adaptive batching that caps concurrency per shard. we'll record p50/p95/99 and error histograms.
09:20 Rajiv: curious — adaptive batching may change throughput profile, please include per-batch-size histograms.
09:26 Maya: yes we'll include that and the per-kernel timing breakdown.
09:32 Dr. Elena: any reason to be concerned about vendor lock-in when using these optimizations?
09:37 Jordan: the optimizations are at serving/runtime level; we provide portable config and a migration plan. the weights and model config remain your assets; the runtime optimizations are Redwood-managed but we give you the rollout tooling and configs so they can be reproduced in private deployment if needed.
09:55 Lisa: great. procurement note: can you write two pricing scenarios — pay-as-you-go vs monthly commit — and show break-even at our expected volume?
10:03 Jordan: yes will send both.
10:07 Rajiv: final technical ask — can you include the raw traces for the spike at 2025-08-29 03:14 UTC where baseline had a 5xx burst? we'd like to compare with our logs.
10:16 Maya: got it, we'll attach those in the perf bundle.
10:20 Dr. Elena: ok let's wrap; thank you very much.
10:24 Jordan: quick recap of next steps — Maya share config/logs by 9/8; Jordan send pricing and contract by 9/6; start 24h soak tomorrow and report by 9/6; schedule deep-dive for 9/10. thanks everyone.
10:38 Lisa: thanks all.
10:42 (call ends)

NOTES: rough transcription with minor name/term errors (e.g., KV cache transcribed as 'KV cash' in earlier automated export), timestamps approximate to segment boundaries. Links referenced: performance spreadsheet (link: drive.redwood/perf/origen-week6), security one-pager (link: drive.redwood/security/origen), demo recording placeholder (link: drive.redwood/recordings/2025-09-04-origen).
